query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled thermal aging of the Mg-containing lightweight HEA drives a metastable-to-intermetallic transformation that degrades its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance. In the as-quenched metastable solid-solution state, the alloy exhibits superior environmental resistance, whereas systematic annealing induces discrete intermetallic precipitation that disrupts the continuity of the protective surface oxide film.
generation.material_initial_state: Non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing Mg-bearing high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Conduct a series of systematic annealing experiments (controlled thermal aging) designed to simulate service conditions, while maintaining a set of as-quenched samples as controls.
generation.conditions: Service-regime conditions featuring corrosive environments and high-temperature oxidation exposures, with annealing temperatures and durations sufficient to initiate diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds.
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation and growth of discrete intermetallic precipitates within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated diffusion processes at service-simulated temperatures lead to the controlled formation of intermetallic phases from the metastable solid solution. This precipitation interferes with the alloy’s ability to form and maintain a protective oxide layer, thereby degrading its corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will show the emergence and coarsening of intermetallic precipitates over time alongside a measurable decrease in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance, in contrast to the as-quenched samples which retain their protective properties.
generation.baseline: The initial as-quenched metastable solid solution state, exhibiting uniform solid-solution microstructure and high resistance to corrosion and oxidation.
generation.boundary: Service conditions defined by corrosive media and high-temperature oxidation; annealing treatments must be within a temperature/time window that is representative of actual industrial operating environments.
generation.uncertainty: Although the general pathway of intermetallic formation is supported by trends in similar systems, the exact kinetics and the critical precipitate density required to trigger noticeable degradation in protective behavior remain to be precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same Mg-containing HEA: one set remains in the as-quenched state and the other is subjected to controlled annealing under service-simulated conditions. Systematically vary the aging time and temperature to promote intermetallic precipitation. Subsequently, compare the microstructural evolution via microscopy and phase analysis alongside corrosion and oxidation performance tests.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (scanning/transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction) to detect and quantify intermetallic precipitates
Electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to assess corrosion resistance
High-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., thermogravimetric analysis) to evaluate oxidation kinetics and mass gain
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If microstructural analysis shows the formation and growth of intermetallic precipitates in the annealed samples with no corresponding decline in corrosion and oxidation resistance, or if both as-quenched and annealed samples exhibit similar performance, the hypothesized mechanistic link must be rejected.

frame.system: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially prepared as a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state with the potential for intermetallic phase formation
frame.goal: To elucidate a single mechanistic hypothesis explaining the microstructural evolution that governs whether the alloy retains or loses its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance during service
frame.limitation: The unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics, especially given the alloy’s tendency to form intermetallic compounds, which has left the link between microstructural shifts and performance degradation unclear
root_cause_cues: tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds
constraints: unnamed controlled comparison (e.g., comparing an annealed sample against one that remains in the as-quenched state)
predicted observations relative to the initial state (e.g., the emergence of discrete intermetallic precipitates accompanied by changes in corrosion/oxidation behavior)
relevant service-regime boundaries (i.e., conditions simulating real-world corrosive and high-temperature oxidation environments)
supporting evidence drawn from reported observations in Mg-containing high-entropy alloys
a clear falsification result (i.e., if the microstructural evolution is observed but no corresponding change in corrosion/oxidation resistance occurs, then the hypothesis must be rejected)
frame.regime: Service conditions characterized by corrosive environments and high-temperature oxidation exposures, defining the operational boundaries within which the alloy’s performance is assessed
prior_attempts: Previous studies have reported the formation of intermetallics in similar Mg-containing high-entropy alloys, yet they have fallen short of directly linking the transformation kinetics with the observed changes in corrosion and oxidation resistance. These studies lack a unified hypothesis that accounts for controlled comparisons and service-level performance shifts.

decision.trend: Early studies in high‐ and complex concentrated alloys first catalogued the microstructures and mechanical properties of metastable solid solutions, showing that under thermal exposures these alloys eventually develop intermetallic precipitates. In particular, lightweight alloy systems (including those with Mg) have demonstrated that after heat-treatment or during service conditions, metastable solid solutions can transform, with observations of discrete intermetallic phases emerging that coincide with degradation in corrosion and oxidation resistance. Subsequent work in refractory HEAs further highlighted that long-duration high-temperature exposures promote intragranular precipitation and phase coarsening, yet a direct link between transformation kinetics and environmental performance remains lacking.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved issue is establishing a mechanistic connection between the kinetics and pathway of the metastable-to-intermetallic transformation and the consequent changes in corrosion/high-temperature oxidation resistance. Specifically, it is unclear how the nucleation and spatial evolution of intermetallic compounds in a Mg-containing lightweight HEA influence the protective properties, given that earlier works did not incorporate a controlled comparative assessment or detailed service-regime testing.
decision.lever: Systematic annealing experiments to compare as-quenched (metastable) versus thermally aged samples under controlled temperature/time schedules that simulate service conditions
decision.why: Building on trends observed in lightweight and refractory HEAs, a direct controlled-variable comparison is the most plausible next step. By designing experiments that deliberately vary aging parameters, researchers can track the onset and progression of intermetallic precipitation and correlate these changes with shifts in corrosion/oxidation behavior. This approach meets the requirement of an unnamed controlled comparison, yields predicted observations relative to the initial state, tests within realistic service-regime boundaries, and provides a clear falsification pathway if microstructural evolution occurs without a concomitant change in environmental resistance.
